lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Life on earth without the Sun

pages.body:
Imagine that the Sun did not rise tomorrow, or the day after, or ever again. The sky stays dark and the air grows colder every hour.

- What would happen to the grass, the crops and the trees?
- What would happen to the animals and the people who depend on those plants?

Every living thing needs energy, and almost all of that energy comes first from the Sun. In this lesson we see why life depends on the Sun and we learn the names given to organisms according to how they get their food.

We begin by tracing what would happen if sunlight stopped reaching the Earth.

pages.title: Life on earth without the Sun
pages.body:
1. Photosynthesis would stop, because green plants and algae need light to make food.
2. Plants would use up their stored food and die. No new oxygen would be released into the air.
3. Herbivores such as grasshoppers, goats and antelopes would starve when the plants died.
4. Carnivores such as snakes, hawks and lions would starve when the herbivores died.
5. The Earth would become extremely cold. Rivers, lakes and finally the sea would freeze.
6. The water cycle would stop, because there would be no heat to evaporate water, so there would be no rain.
7. In the end almost all life on the Earth would die out.
The Sun is therefore the primary source of energy for nearly every ecosystem. It supplies light for photosynthesis and heat that keeps the Earth warm enough for life.

Next we meet the organisms that bring the energy of the Sun into the ecosystem.

## Producers

A producer is an organism that makes its own food from simple substances. Green plants and algae are producers. They use the green pigment chlorophyll to trap light energy and use it to join carbon dioxide and water into glucose. This process is photosynthesis. The light energy is changed to chemical energy stored in the food. Producers are also called autotrophs. Grass, maize, cassava, mango trees and the tiny floating algae in a pond are all producers.

**Carbon dioxide + water, with light energy and chlorophyll, gives glucose + oxygen**

Now we look at the organisms that cannot make their own food.

pages.title: Consumers
pages.body:
A consumer is an organism that gets its food by eating other organisms. All animals are consumers. They are also called heterotrophs. Consumers are grouped by the level at which they feed.

| **Type of consumer** | **What it feeds on** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|
| Primary consumer | Producers. It is a herbivore | Grasshopper, caterpillar, goat, rabbit, grasscutter, tadpole |
| Secondary consumer | Primary consumers. It is a carnivore or an omnivore | Toad, lizard, chicken, small fish, spider |
| Tertiary consumer | Secondary consumers | Snake, hawk, eagle, crocodile |

A herbivore eats only plants, a carnivore eats only animals and an omnivore eats both. A predator is an animal that hunts and kills other animals, and the animal it hunts is its prey. A scavenger, such as a vulture, feeds on animals that are already dead.

Finally we add the organisms that clean up the ecosystem.

pages.title: Decomposers
pages.body:
Decomposers are bacteria and fungi that feed on dead plants, dead animals and waste. They break these down into simple substances such as mineral salts and return them to the soil, where producers take them up again. Without decomposers, dead bodies and waste would pile up and the soil would run out of nutrients.

> **Did you know?** A few ecosystems on the deep sea floor do not depend on the Sun. Bacteria there make food using energy from chemicals that come out of hot vents in the sea bed.

What is a producer? Give two examples.

pages.body:
On a farm, a grasshopper eats maize leaves. A toad eats the grasshopper. A snake eats the toad, and a hawk swoops down and eats the snake.

- Where did the energy in the body of the hawk first come from?
- What would happen to the toads if all the grasshoppers were killed with insecticide?

Feeding links organisms together and passes energy from one to the next. In this lesson we learn to draw food chains and food webs and to explain how energy flows through them.

We start with the simplest way of showing a feeding relationship.

pages.title: Food chains
pages.body:
A food chain is a simple sequence that shows how food energy passes from one organism to the next. It always begins with a producer. Each arrow means is eaten by, and it points in the direction in which the energy moves, from the food to the feeder.

**Sun to maize to grasshopper to toad to snake to hawk**

| **Organism** | **Role in the food chain** | **Trophic level** |
|---|---|---|
| Maize | Producer | First |
| Grasshopper | Primary consumer | Second |
| Toad | Secondary consumer | Third |
| Snake | Tertiary consumer | Fourth |
| Hawk | Top consumer | Fifth |

Each feeding level in a food chain is called a trophic level. Food chains exist in every habitat.

- On land, grass to grasshopper to lizard to hawk.
- In a pond, algae to tadpole to small fish to kingfisher.
- In the sea, tiny floating plants to tiny floating animals to herring to tuna to shark.
- On a tree, leaves to caterpillar to small bird to snake.

Next we see why a single food chain does not tell the whole story.

pages.title: Food webs
pages.body:
Most organisms eat more than one kind of food and are eaten by more than one kind of feeder. A food web is a network of food chains that are linked together in an ecosystem. In a farm ecosystem, maize may be eaten by grasshoppers, rats and weaver birds. The rats may be eaten by snakes and owls, and the grasshoppers by toads, lizards and chickens.

[[pic: Food web of a farm showing the Sun, maize and grass as producers, grasshopper, rat and weaver bird as primary consumers, toad, lizard and chicken as secondary consumers, and snake, owl and hawk as higher consumers, with arrows pointing from each food to its feeder.]]

A food web is more stable than a single food chain. If one kind of food becomes scarce, a consumer in a web can switch to another. A change in one part of the web still affects the others. If farmers kill all the snakes, the number of rats rises and more maize is eaten. If the grasshoppers are poisoned, the toads and lizards have less food and the poison may also pass to the birds that eat them.

Finally we follow the energy itself and see why it becomes less at each level.

## How energy flows

Producers trap only a small part of the light energy that falls on them. When a grasshopper eats a maize leaf, it does not pass on all the energy to the toad that eats it. Most of the energy is used by the grasshopper for moving, growing and other life processes, and is lost to the surroundings as heat. Some leaves the body in waste. Only about one tenth of the energy at one trophic level is passed on to the next level.

| **Trophic level** | **Example** | **Energy available, if producers hold 10 000 units** |
|---|---|---|
| Producers | Maize | 10 000 units |
| Primary consumers | Grasshoppers | About 1 000 units |
| Secondary consumers | Toads | About 100 units |
| Tertiary consumers | Snakes | About 10 units |

- Energy flows in one direction only, from the Sun to producers and then to consumers. It is not recycled.
- The amount of energy becomes smaller at each level, so food chains are short, usually with four or five links.
- There are many more producers than herbivores, and many more herbivores than top carnivores. A drawing of this is called a pyramid of numbers or a pyramid of energy.
- Nutrients such as carbon and nitrogen, unlike energy, are recycled by decomposers.

[[pic: Energy pyramid with four layers. The wide base is labelled producers, followed by primary consumers, secondary consumers and tertiary consumers at the narrow top, with arrows at the side showing heat lost at each level.]]
> **Did you know?** Because energy is lost at every step, a piece of land can feed far more people if they eat the crops directly than if they eat animals that were fed on those crops.

questions.q: Define a food chain and a food web.
Write a food chain with four organisms from a pond and name the producer and the secondary consumer.
What does an arrow in a food chain show?
Explain why a food chain rarely has more than five links.
Predict two effects on a farm food web if all the snakes are killed.

pages.body:
- The Sun is the primary source of energy for almost all ecosystems. Without it photosynthesis would stop, the Earth would freeze and nearly all life would die.
- A producer makes its own food by photosynthesis. Green plants and algae are producers.
- A consumer feeds on other organisms. A primary consumer eats producers, a secondary consumer eats primary consumers and a tertiary consumer eats secondary consumers.
- Decomposers are bacteria and fungi that break down dead organisms and waste and return nutrients to the soil.
- A food chain shows how energy passes from a producer through a series of consumers. The arrows point from the food to the feeder.
- A food web is a network of linked food chains. It is more stable than a single chain, but a change in one part affects the other parts.
- Energy flows in one direction and only about one tenth passes from one trophic level to the next. The rest is used by the organism or lost as heat.
